text: During an access review you find a contractor who left months ago still listed on two repositories. Which control would have prevented it?

options.text: Requiring 2FA for all organization members.
options.why: 2FA hardens authentication for people who should still have access. It does nothing about access that should have been removed.

options.text: SCIM deprovisioning driven by the identity provider, so leaving the IdP removes the GitHub account.
options.why: Manual offboarding is where stale access comes from. SCIM ties the account lifecycle to the IdP, so a leaver is deprovisioned automatically — which also frees the licence.

options.text: Branch protection on the default branch.
options.why: A merge policy. It constrains what an account can land, not whether the account should exist.

options.text: Moving the repositories into a different organization.
options.why: Access follows the grant, not the location.

takeaway: Stale access is an offboarding failure. SCIM automates deprovisioning; periodic access review catches what slips through.

text: Which practices are recommended when scripting permission management across many organizations? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Build scripts in modular components so a new organization needs minimal change.
options.why: Yes — modularity is what keeps the automation maintainable as the estate grows.

options.text: Test in a controlled environment before deploying.
options.why: Yes. A permissions script run against production untested can revoke access at scale.

options.text: Log changes in detail, and keep the scripts under version control.
options.why: Yes — logging supports troubleshooting and compliance, and version control gives review and rollback for the automation itself.

options.text: Run scripts with an organization owner's personal access token for simplicity.
options.why: No. That ties enterprise automation to one person's credential — a GitHub App with fine-grained permissions is the appropriate identity.

takeaway: Modular, tested, logged, version-controlled — and authenticated as an App rather than a person.

text: Developers report intermittent API failures during business hours. Investigation shows several third-party integrations polling continuously. What is the primary risk being described?

options.text: The integrations are consuming enterprise licences, raising cost.
options.why: True of machine accounts and worth auditing, but it does not cause intermittent failures for developers.

options.text: Excessive API calls exhaust rate limits, which then affects developers' workflows.
options.why: Heavy polling by third-party tools and CI/CD consumes shared API capacity. The stated consequence is exactly this: excessive calls lead to rate limits that affect developer workflows. The remedy is to replace polling with webhooks, Apps or Actions triggers.

options.text: Audit log retention is being exceeded.
options.why: Retention governs how long events are kept, not API availability.

options.text: Secret scanning is throttling the integrations.
options.why: Secret scanning does not rate-limit API consumers.

takeaway: Avoid inefficient polling. Use webhooks, GitHub Apps or Actions to trigger automation, and monitor API usage for unknown consumers.

text: Match the token type to its use: a one-off maintenance script, a GitHub App integration, and renewing expired access without re-authenticating.

options.text: PAT, installation token, refresh token respectively.
options.why: PATs are tied to a user account and suit simple scripts. Installation tokens serve GitHub App installations with fine-grained permissions. Refresh tokens renew expired tokens without requiring the user to authenticate again.

options.text: Installation token, PAT, device token respectively.
options.why: The first two are swapped, and device tokens serve device-based authentication flows.

options.text: OAuth token, refresh token, PAT respectively.
options.why: OAuth tokens serve OAuth Apps with scoped access; none of this mapping holds.

options.text: Device token, OAuth token, installation token respectively.
options.why: None of these match their stated use.

takeaway: PAT = user-tied, simple scripts, broad scope. Installation = App, fine-grained. OAuth = scoped, on behalf of a user. Refresh = renew without re-auth.

text: After approving a third-party app, what ongoing review does the guidance call for?

options.text: None — approval is a one-time decision.
options.why: An app's access and the events it receives can matter long after approval, and the tool itself may fall out of use.

options.text: Manage and regularly review the app's event subscriptions and continued necessity.
options.why: OAuth Apps should be granted least privilege with event subscriptions managed and reviewed regularly. Auditing third-party tools also identifies integrations no longer in use, which reduces both risk and cost.

options.text: Rotate the organization's SAML certificate each time an app is added.
options.why: Unrelated to application authorisation.

options.text: Convert every approved OAuth App into a machine account.
options.why: That would consume licences and reintroduce a user-tied credential.

takeaway: App approval is not permanent. Review subscriptions, least privilege and whether the integration is still needed.

text: You must stop public repositories using the enterprise's self-hosted runners while keeping them available to selected internal repositories. What do you configure?

options.text: An IP allow list on the runner hosts.
options.why: IP allow lists restrict network reachability. They do not express which repositories may schedule jobs.

options.text: A runner group with access limited to selected repositories, and public repositories excluded.
options.why: Runner groups are the access boundary: create the group, set the access level to allow only selected repositories, and do not allow public repositories to use enterprise runners.

options.text: Ephemeral runners, which refuse public repository jobs.
options.why: Ephemeral means the runner resets after each job. It is an isolation property, not an access rule.

options.text: Branch protection on each public repository.
options.why: A merge control with no bearing on runner scheduling.

takeaway: Runner groups scope which repositories and teams may use runners. IP allow lists control who can reach them. Ephemeral controls reuse.

text: Jobs queue for long periods on self-hosted runners during peak hours, while GitHub-hosted jobs elsewhere start immediately. What explains the difference?

options.text: Self-hosted runners are rate-limited by GitHub during peak periods.
options.why: No such throttle exists; capacity is whatever you have provisioned.

options.text: GitHub-hosted runners autoscale dynamically, whereas self-hosted capacity must be provisioned manually.
options.why: Autoscaling is a GitHub-hosted property. With self-hosted runners you add capacity yourself, so a fixed pool queues under peak load — which is what monitoring runner performance is meant to surface.

options.text: Self-hosted runners only accept jobs from the default branch.
options.why: No such restriction.

options.text: The workflows are missing a concurrency group.
options.why: Concurrency limits overlap deliberately; it would cause queuing you configured, not a capacity shortfall.

takeaway: Hosted runners autoscale; self-hosted do not. Queue depth against a fixed pool is a provisioning signal.

text: Which statement about where a secret becomes available is correct?

options.text: Every secret is available to every workflow in the organization once created.
options.why: That would defeat scoping entirely. Availability follows the level at which the secret is defined.

options.text: A secret is accessible to workflows and actions with permission to the organization, repository or environment where it is defined.
options.why: Secrets are encrypted environment variables, and access follows the definition level. Choosing that level is the scoping decision — organization for shared credentials, repository for local ones, environment for deployment-gated ones.

options.text: Repository secrets override organization secrets of the same name and are visible in logs.
options.why: Secrets are masked in logs; printing them is what you actively guard against.

options.text: Environment secrets are available to any job in the repository.
options.why: They are available to jobs targeting that environment, which is precisely the point of using them for production.

takeaway: Definition level determines availability: organization, repository, or environment. Scope to the lowest level that works.

text: A workflow fetches a database password from HashiCorp Vault at run time. What still has to live in GitHub, and why does the arrangement help?

options.text: Nothing — Vault integration removes all GitHub secrets.
options.why: The Vault action authenticates with a token, typically referenced as a GitHub secret. Only OIDC genuinely removes the stored credential.

options.text: A Vault token as a GitHub secret; the database password itself stays in Vault, where it can be rotated and audited centrally.
options.why: One credential in GitHub replaces many. The password lives in Vault with automated rotation, access control and audit logging, and least-privilege access means the workflow retrieves only what it needs.

options.text: The database password, duplicated in GitHub as a fallback.
options.why: Duplicating the secret reintroduces exactly the exposure the vault was adopted to remove.

options.text: Nothing, because Vault actions authenticate anonymously.
options.why: Vault requires authentication.

takeaway: Vaults collapse many stored secrets into one authentication credential, and add rotation plus audit. OIDC removes even that.

text: Which are explicitly the administrator's responsibility rather than GitHub Support's? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Infrastructure configuration and hardware setup.
options.why: Yes — named as administrator scope, particularly for self-hosted GHES.

options.text: CI/CD integrations and internal scripting.
options.why: Yes. Support does not debug your pipelines or automation.

options.text: Third-party authentication systems such as SAML.
options.why: Yes — configuring and troubleshooting the IdP integration is the administrator's job.

options.text: Investigating harassment reports under GitHub's terms of service.
options.why: No — abuse cases are one of Support's three named areas, alongside accounts and security.

takeaway: Support: accounts, security, abuse. Administrators: infrastructure, internal tooling, CI/CD, external auth, immediate on-prem response.

text: A credential was committed and pushed six months ago. Rewriting history to remove it is planned. What else is essential?

options.text: Nothing further — removing it from history fully resolves the exposure.
options.why: The credential has been readable for six months. History rewriting removes the copy, not the knowledge of it.

options.text: Rotate the credential, because it must be assumed compromised regardless of the rewrite.
options.why: Anything committed and pushed should be treated as disclosed — it may exist in clones, forks and caches. Rotation is the control that actually ends the exposure; the rewrite is cleanup. Note that clearing caches after history rewriting is a task requiring GitHub Support.

options.text: Enable branch protection so it cannot happen again.
options.why: Sensible hardening, but it does not address the already-exposed credential. Push protection is the preventive control for secrets.

options.text: Delete and recreate the repository.
options.why: Destroys history and collaboration while still leaving the leaked credential valid.

takeaway: A pushed secret is a compromised secret. Rotate first, then clean history — and enable push protection so the next one never lands.

text: An enterprise wants a set of vetted, centrally maintained workflows that any organization can call. Where should they live?

options.text: Duplicated into every repository that needs them, kept in sync by a bot.
options.why: Synchronised duplication is still duplication, with a new failure mode when the bot drifts or breaks.

options.text: In a designated enterprise repository, referenced as reusable workflows by callers.
options.why: Centralising vetted actions and workflows in an enterprise repository and calling them is what makes reuse manageable — one place to review, update and secure, with every caller inheriting the change.

options.text: In each developer's personal account, shared by link.
options.why: Ties enterprise automation to individual accounts, which disappear when people leave.

options.text: As a Marketplace action published publicly.
options.why: Publishing internal build logic publicly is an unnecessary disclosure, and it does not give the enterprise control over consumption.

takeaway: Vet centrally, reuse widely: enterprise-owned repository plus reusable workflows, governed by Actions policy.
